article.title: Uniting the Left
article.author: Sharon Kyle, Eric Mann, Vincent De Stefano, Dick Price, Robert Corsini
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. What happens when a room full of people who want to change the world cannot agree on how to change it? That question hung over a spirited roundtable discussion titled "Uniting the Left" at the 2026 Left Coast Forum, held October 2–4 at California State University, Los Angeles. The gathering brought together activists, organizers, political thinkers and representatives of progressive organizations to confront a problem that has frustrated the American left for generations: Despite widespread dissatisfaction with political and economic conditions, progressive movements remain fragmented, often struggling to translate their collective numbers into political power. The panel featured Ben Cohen, co-founder of Ben & Jerry's; veteran civil rights organizer Eric Mann; LA Progressive publisher and Left Coast Forum co-founder Sharon Kyle; former Santa Monica Rent Control Board chair Ericka Lesley; and longtime peace and social justice activist Vincent De Stefano. Their common objective was straightforward: explore the possibility of creating a united front among organizations participating in the forum. But as the discussion unfolded, it became apparent that agreement on the need for unity was considerably easier than agreement on what unity would require. Can There Be Unity Without Racial Justice? Kyle opened the discussion by questioning why progressive organizations, despite their numbers and shared concerns, have been unable to exercise greater influence over national policy. Sharon Kyle Pointing to federal layoffs, attacks on diversity initiatives, reductions in public assistance and aggressive immigration enforcement, she argued that the left needs something more consequential than expressions of solidarity. It needs power. Kyle suggested that racial division has historically enabled concentrated economic power to survive by preventing working people from recognizing and acting upon their common interests. Drawing on Republican strategist Lee Atwater's notorious explanation of the Southern Strategy, she described how explicitly racist political appeals evolved into seemingly race-neutral language involving taxes, government spending and social programs. The resulting policies, she argued, can preserve racial hierarchies even when politicians avoid explicitly mentioning race. For Kyle, the question was not simply how organizations could unite around shared economic interests, but whether they could meaningfully confront the racial divisions that have repeatedly undermined efforts at solidarity. Eric Mann Mann, director of the Labor/Community Strategy Center and a veteran of the civil rights movement, challenged the assumption that the fundamental political struggle could be reduced to the 99 percent against the wealthiest 1 percent. He argued that racism is not merely a tool wielded by economic elites against an otherwise unified working class. White Americans, including members of the working class, have historically participated in and benefited from systems of racial domination. Mann's analysis centered the United States' history of settler colonialism, slavery and imperialism. Drawing on his decades of organizing, including work with the Congress of Racial Equality and in Black communities during the 1960s, he argued that the progressive movement must place Black political power at the center of its strategy. "We don't need DEI, although it's good. We need Black power," Mann declared. He also questioned whether electoral victories, even those involving politicians he admires, could produce fundamental transformation without stronger independent social movements. For Mann, the immediate priority was not capturing the presidency but building organizations capable of advancing demands that conventional electoral politics routinely excludes. Ben Cohen Offers a Plan for 2028 While Mann emphasized the limitations of electoral politics, Ben Cohen presented a proposal designed to influence the next presidential election. Introducing an initiative he called "Citizens in Search of a Candidate," Cohen described a broad, multi-issue people's platform built around demands that already enjoy substantial public support. Ben Cohen His premise was that progressive organizations have divided themselves into separate movements for racial justice, environmental protection, immigrant rights, economic equality, housing and peace. Each movement struggles against powerful institutional opponents, yet they often fail to combine their strength. "None of us can succeed alone. We can all succeed together," Cohen told the gathering. His proposal would bring organizations together to develop a common platform encompassing such priorities as removing money from politics, establishing living wages, expanding affordable housing and childcare, providing universal healthcare, protecting the environment, ending endless wars and redirecting excessive military spending toward human needs. Rather than beginning with a preferred presidential candidate, the movement would first establish its demands and then seek to influence candidates competing for public support. Cohen envisioned a national listening tour, media campaigns, participation by social media influencers and potentially millions of people signing onto the platform. The objective was to make ordinary people, rather than corporate donors, the driving force behind the political agenda. Cohen also challenged the familiar argument that the United States cannot afford expansive social programs. He introduced a video using Oreo cookies to illustrate the scale of military spending and what comparable resources could accomplish if redirected toward housing, education, healthcare and other public needs. The presentation offered a vivid illustration of the choices underlying federal budget priorities. But Cohen's proposal also raised a difficult question: Could organizations with fundamentally different political analyses agree on a common platform without suppressing their disagreements? Representation Is Not the Same as Power Ericka Lesley brought a different perspective to the discussion, drawing on her experience as a Black woman in local government and as someone who had personally experienced homelessness. Erika Lesley Lesley, who served on the Santa Monica Rent Control Board and became its first Black woman chair, described the obstacles she encountered while attempting to represent communities historically excluded from political decision-making. Her message challenged organizations that celebrate diversity while failing to support the leadership of people of color. "We can't just request people of color's labor without also supporting their leadership," she said. Lesley argued that people who identify racial inequities can themselves become targets of hostility, including within institutions that profess commitments to fairness and inclusion. Her critique extended beyond electoral representation. She described wage theft, union busting and failures of solidarity among organizations supposedly pursuing similar objectives. "We are not in a time of allyship. We are in a time of co-conspiracy," she declared. The distinction was significant. Allyship can imply sympathy or support from a distance. What Lesley called for was active participation in struggles against injustice, including a willingness to challenge established power relationships. She also questioned why some international conflicts command sustained attention among American progressives while others receive comparatively little discussion. Pointing to violence in Ethiopia, she argued that African suffering should not become secondary to struggles elsewhere. Her intervention illustrated a recurring problem for coalition-building: Even organizations committed to universal human rights may differ sharply over which crises deserve immediate attention and resources. Finding Common Ground Without Erasing Differences Vincent De Stefano, a longtime activist associated with Assange Defense and Amnesty International, emphasized the potential strength of a movement willing to set aside sectarian disputes. The political and economic establishment, he suggested, possesses enormous advantages in wealth, media influence and institutional power. Ordinary people, however, possess numbers. Vincent De Stefano De Stefano argued that organizations could build greater influence by identifying common demands, including healthcare, opposition to war and civil liberties, even where participants disagree on broader political questions. The audience soon demonstrated both the appeal and complexity of that approach. Former Santa Monica Mayor Mike Feinstein argued that a progressive platform would accomplish little without changes to the electoral system itself. He advocated proportional representation and ranked-choice voting, suggesting that structural reforms could allow independent political movements to compete more effectively. Other participants proposed Social Security protection as a potentially unifying demand, challenged the progressive movement's approach to nuclear energy, called for stronger attention to African conflicts and urged greater leadership by people of color. One participant warned that creating another nonprofit organization would not solve the left's underlying problems. Instead, he urged greater investment in existing grassroots organizations and stronger opportunities for young activists to assume leadership. These contributions underscored the central dilemma: A movement expansive enough to include different constituencies must also develop ways to make decisions when those constituencies disagree. An especially revealing exchange followed an audience member's question about the possibility of building alliances across political differences. Mann responded that the purpose of a united front should not be to persuade everyone to abandon their political positions. "Nobody should try to win the argument," he said. Instead, he urged participants to respect their differences, listen to one another and identify opportunities for cooperation. That may have been one of the discussion's most practical observations. Unity need not require ideological uniformity. But it does require a willingness to recognize where cooperation is possible—and where disagreements cannot simply be wished away. From Conversation to Political Power The discussion did not conclude with the announcement of a formal united front, an agreed organizational structure or a binding set of commitments among participating groups. What emerged instead was a clearer picture of the work such an undertaking would require. Cohen's proposed platform offered a possible mechanism for organizing around common demands. Mann insisted that independent movements and the struggle against racial domination remain central. Lesley challenged progressives to examine whose leadership they support in practice. Kyle pressed participants to confront racial division as an obstacle to collective power. De Stefano emphasized the practical necessity of cooperation. Together, their contributions exposed a problem that cannot be resolved by simply assembling more organizations under a common banner. A united front would have to determine how decisions are made, whose priorities receive attention, how leadership is shared, how disagreements are resolved and what participating organizations are actually prepared to do together. Near the session's conclusion, former Ohio State Senator Nina Turner briefly addressed the gathering, reinforcing the importance of ordinary people taking responsibility for political change. "Nobody with a special title is coming to save us," she reminded the audience. The remark captured the challenge facing the participants. The American left does not lack organizations, ideas, grievances or committed activists. What it has struggled to develop is the collective capacity to turn those resources into sustained political power. The Left Coast Forum's "Uniting the Left" discussion offered no easy formula for overcoming that weakness. But it accomplished something important: It placed the movement's internal divisions, strategic disagreements and unresolved questions of leadership squarely on the table. Perhaps that is where meaningful unity must begin—not with declarations that differences no longer matter, but with the difficult work of confronting them. Watch the full discussion: Uniting the Left — Left Coast Forum 2026 .
